minus: The framework is evaluated on an integrated 108-bus transmission--distribution test system over a 15-year horizon. Without shared storage, coordination reduces discounted operating costs by 12.2\% relative to a price-taker benchmark that prohibits reverse active-power flow from distribution to transmission. Under the baseline assumptions, none of the evaluated storage plans recovers its investment cost. For a fixed reference 0.25~MVA/1~MWh unit, baseline ageing yields an investment shortfall of 64.4~k\euro{}, while the margin without ageing is within numerical resolution of break-even. The unit achieves positive investment margins at 1.75 and 2 times the base flexibility price. Its estimated margin remains negative in the $3 \times 3$ multi-scenario evaluation.

minus: \item \textcolor{blue}{A two-stage stochastic planning framework for shared ESS deployment at TN--DN interface nodes, in which one scenario-independent investment plan is evaluated against coordinated TSO--DSO operation; in this study the planning searches run on a single operating scenario and fixed plans are evaluated under market and operation scenarios.}

\item \textcolor{blue}{A degradation-aware shared ESS formulation that internalizes cycling- and calendar-induced capacity loss, calibrated from datasheet cycle-life statements and bounded by an end-of-life floor, and preserves the intertemporal consistency of available storage capacity.}

\item \textcolor{blue}{A nested solution strategy combining a derivative-free investment search with ADMM-based decentralized operational evaluation, together with explicit numerical acceptance criteria for assessing the resolution of planning comparisons.}

\item \textcolor{blue}{A case study on an integrated 108-bus system that quantifies the value of coordination against static interface practice, the break-even conditions for shared storage in energy cost and flexibility price, and the effect of degradation on storage value and available capacity.}
plus: \item \textcolor{blue}{A two-stage stochastic planning framework for shared ESS deployment at TN--DN interface nodes, considering coordinated TSO--DSO operation while maintaining institutional independence.}

\item \textcolor{blue}{A degradation-aware formulation that represents the energy capacity lost to cycling and to calendar ageing, linking storage dispatch to the capacity available over the planning horizon.}

\item \textcolor{blue}{A nested solution strategy in which a derivative-free search over investment plans is combined with a decentralized, ADMM-based evaluation of coordinated TSO--DSO operation, every reported comparison being stated with its numerical resolution.}

\item \textcolor{blue}{A case study on an integrated 108-bus system that quantifies the value of coordinated operation, the break-even conditions for shared storage in energy cost and flexibility price, and the effect of degradation on storage value and available capacity.}

minus: %The results show that coordinated planning and operation with shared ESSs yield substantial system-wide benefits, including lower operating costs, improved RES integration, and mitigation of voltage violations observed under uncoordinated operation. They also show that explicitly representing degradation materially affects ESS valuation and long-term investment outcomes, while planning-horizon discretization can influence degradation trajectories and, consequently, ESS siting and sizing decisions.
Under the baseline assumptions, the planning search returned the plan without shared storage, $\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{0}$.

None of its fourteen admissible unit neighbours reduced total discounted cost beyond the search resolution; the result applies to the evaluated neighbourhood. Because the operating cost was found to vary almost linearly with installed capacity over the evaluated plans (Subsection~\ref{subsec:res_breakeven}), the capacity ladders below carry the planning information: the search returns a corner of the admissible set, and the ladders show why.

Table~\ref{tab:res_value_ladder} shows that the reference unit, comprising 0.25~MVA and 1~MWh installed at node~7 in 2025, provides discounted operating savings of 253.5~k\euro{} against an investment cost of 318.0~k\euro{}. Its total discounted cost exceeds that of the plan without storage by 64.4~k\euro{}. The smallest admissible unit at node~5, comprising 0.25~MVA and 0.5~MWh, increases total cost by 49.7~k\euro{}. Both cost increases are determinate.
plus: Under the baseline assumptions, no shared storage investment recovers its cost. The search returned the plan without storage, and none of its fourteen admissible unit neighbours reduces the total discounted cost.

Table~\ref{tab:res_value_ladder} reports the cost increase of selected plans: the reference unit, 0.25~MVA and 1~MWh at node~7 in 2025, saves 253.5 k\euro{} in operation against an investment of 318.0 k\euro{}, a shortfall of 64.4 k\euro{}; larger units, longer durations and two-node plans lose more. Because the operating cost varies almost linearly with installed capacity over the evaluated plans (Subsection~\ref{subsec:res_breakeven}), the capacity ladders carry the planning information: the search returns a corner of the admissible set, and the ladders show why.

The planning question was also tested directly: the fourteen admissible unit neighbours of the plan without storage were evaluated under the no-ageing calibration with the production stopping rule, as a planning search would evaluate them. None reduces the total discounted cost; eight are more expensive beyond the search's acceptance threshold and six lie within it, with cost increases from 2.7 to 100.6~k\euro{}. Without ageing, therefore, the search would also stop at the plan without storage, and at this resolution it cannot discriminate the smallest storage units from no storage; with ageing, every unit neighbour is determinately worse (Subsection~\ref{subsec:res_baseline}). The comparison is a bounded screen of the unit neighbourhood at the base flexibility price, not a completed search.

minus: Two requests were not met in full. We did not attribute degradation separately to the TSO and the DSO (Reviewer~1): the shared ESS follows a jointly determined schedule and no unique attribution exists; a marginal or Shapley-type allocation is identified as future work. We did not re-optimize the investment plan under every ageing calibration (Reviewer~3, degradation-neutral benchmark): the ageing comparison of Section~4.3 re-evaluates a fixed plan, so it establishes the effect of degradation on storage value and available capacity, not on the selected plan; under the no-ageing calibration the reference unit's margin is within the numerical resolution of zero, so its sign is not resolved. The planning part of this request is therefore met only in part, and the paper says so (Section~4.7). The largest instance of the submitted version (five representative years, twenty-five scenarios) could not be evaluated under the certification rule within the memory available and is stated as future work (Section~4.7); the multi-scenario results are given on a $3\times3$ scenario instance (Section~4.5).
plus: Two requests were not met in full. We did not attribute degradation separately to the TSO and the DSO (Reviewer~1): the shared ESS follows a jointly determined schedule and no unique attribution exists; a marginal or Shapley-type allocation is identified as future work.

We did not re-optimize the investment plan under every ageing calibration (Reviewer~3, degradation-neutral benchmark): the ageing comparison of Section~4.3 re-evaluates a fixed plan, and the planning part of the request was met at the scale the method allows, a screen of the fourteen unit neighbours of the plan without storage under the no-ageing calibration, which returns the same plan (Section~4.3); a full degradation-neutral search over the lattice was not run, and the paper says so (Section~4.7).

The largest instance of the submitted version (five representative years, twenty-five scenarios) could not be evaluated under the certification rule within the memory available and is stated as future work (Section~4.7); the multi-scenario results are given on a $3\times3$ scenario instance (Section~4.5).

minus: Beyond the Reviewers' requests, the revision adds two robustness checks. The coordinated arrangement was re-evaluated with the same no-reverse-flow restriction that the static benchmarks carry: the restriction costs 20.5~k\euro{}, 0.02\,\% of the 90.9~M\euro{} saving, so the reported 12.2\,\% benefit does not depend on the interface rule. The two decisive storage comparisons were re-evaluated with the coordination penalties halved and doubled: every sign and verdict is unchanged, and the differences move by about a tenth of their determinacy threshold. 4.3.text: The planning question was also tested directly: the fourteen admissible unit neighbours of the plan without storage were evaluated under the no-ageing calibration with the production stopping rule, as a planning search would evaluate them. None reduces the total discounted cost; eight are more expensive beyond the search's acceptance threshold and six lie within it, with cost increases from 2.7 to 100.6~k\euro{}. Without ageing, therefore, the search would also stop at the plan without storage, and at this resolution it cannot discriminate the smallest storage units from no storage; with ageing, every unit neighbour is determinately worse (Subsection~\ref{subsec:res_baseline}). The comparison is a bounded screen of the unit neighbourhood at the base flexibility price, not a completed search.

texts.59: We did not re-optimize the investment plan under every ageing calibration (Reviewer~3, degradation-neutral benchmark): the ageing comparison of Section~4.3 re-evaluates a fixed plan, and the planning part of the request was met at the scale the method allows, a screen of the fourteen unit neighbours of the plan without storage under the no-ageing calibration, which returns the same plan (Section~4.3); a full degradation-neutral search over the lattice was not run, and the paper says so (Section~4.7).
texts.264: Under the no-ageing calibration the unit’s margin is within the numerical resolution of zero, so its sign is not resolved. The planning part of the request was then met at the scale the method allows: the fourteen admissible unit neighbours of the plan without storage were evaluated under the no-ageing calibration as a planning search would evaluate them (Section~4.3). None reduces the total discounted cost --- eight are worse beyond the search’s acceptance threshold and six within it --- so a degradation-neutral search would return the same plan; what degradation changes at this scale is the margin by which the storage units lose, not the selected plan. A full degradation-neutral search over the lattice was not run.
texts.263: Lowering the end-of-life floor from 0.70 to 0.50 changes the value by $+4.9$~k\euro{}, within resolution: at this precision no effect of the floor on the value is resolved (Table~6, last row). On installed capacity and timing: under every aged calibration the reference unit loses determinately; the search was not rerun per calibration, so the comparison establishes the valuation effect of degradation at a fixed plan, and the unit-neighbourhood screen its effect on the selected plan (Section~4.3).

cover.text: A degradation-neutral evaluation of the unit neighbourhood of the plan without storage is also reported (Section~4.3): without ageing the search would return the same plan.

texts.1374: Under the baseline assumptions, no shared storage investment recovers its cost. The search returned the plan without storage, and none of its fourteen admissible unit neighbours reduces the total discounted cost.
texts.1375: Table~\ref{tab:res_value_ladder} reports the cost increase of selected plans: the reference unit, 0.25~MVA and 1~MWh at node~7 in 2025, saves 253.5 k\euro{} in operation against an investment of 318.0 k\euro{}, a shortfall of 64.4 k\euro{}; larger units, longer durations and two-node plans lose more. Because the operating cost varies almost linearly with installed capacity over the evaluated plans (Subsection~\ref{subsec:res_breakeven}), the capacity ladders carry the planning information: the search returns a corner of the admissible set, and the ladders show why.
